pairing.scope: Compare covers the 1,257 images both arms read; Sonnet 5 stopped at 1,258.
pairing.only_text: Sonnet 5.5 alone, no Sonnet 5 reading: 258 images, Sonnet 5.5 257 exact (99.6%), CXMolScribe 212 (82.2%). Not in any Sonnet 5 vs 5.5 figure.

protocol.why: Cost. A ten-image reader re-reads its whole growing context on every step, so a batch of heavy molecules snowballs: one Sonnet 5.5 reader on ten large gap molecules cost $11.06 (35M cache-read tokens, 144 tool calls) against a $2.30 estimate. One image per reader caps that, lets the cadence predict each reader's cost from the molecule's size, and lets it stop a runaway reader without losing nine other readings.
protocol.prompt_change: The single-image prompts are the arms' ten-image prompts with only the image count changed: 'reading one chemical structure image ... the molecule it depicts', 'The image is:', 'Read the image yourself', 'Write the one entry, fig01'. Every other word, both integrity paragraphs, the sandbox, the exact-model check and the gate are unchanged.
protocol.pairing: From this switch, while both arms were reading, each new image was read by both in its own single-image reader, Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5 started together, so each pair completed together. The rows before it were read ten to a reader, with batch-mates in the same context.
protocol.text: Single-image readers from row 1071 of the Sonnet 5.5 arm and row 1077 of the Sonnet 5 arm (2026-10-02): one image per reader; until Sonnet 5 stopped (2026-10-04) both models read each new image at the same time. Earlier rows were read 10 images to a reader, in one shared context.

batches.1: 6 images Sonnet 5 read wrong plus 2 controls it read right (ezetimibe, febuxostat).
batches.2: 14 Sonnet 5 misses spread across failure types (4 connectivity, 4 stereo-only, 5 atom count, 1 wrong element) plus the 6 Sonnet 5 exact reads with the lowest numeric confidence (18-55). Two readers of ten per model. Two Sonnet 5 re-run readers of the same ten images were discarded unscored: one handed 7 of its 10 images to sub-agents served by Opus 5.5, the next hit an API usage limit before writing any answer. A third, fresh Sonnet 5 reader read them.

runs.prompt:
You are reading eight chemical structure images and writing down the molecule each one depicts, as SMILES.

The images are:
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig01.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig02.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig03.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig04.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig05.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig06.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig07.png
/tmp/blinds55_b/fig08.png

NO LOOKUPS. This is a blind test, and its answer key comes from public chemistry databases, so any lookup voids the reading. Do NOT look up any structure in PubChem, KEGG, ChEMBL, ChemSpider or any online database or name-to-structure service; do not use WebFetch or web search or fetch anything over the network except to install a tool from a package manager; do not read any file other than the images you were given, your own scratch files and the tools you run. Local tools (RDKit, image processing, OSRA, recognising the molecule) are fine. Write the answers to /tmp/answerss55_b.json as a JSON array [{"img","smiles","name_if_recognised","confidence"}].

Guidance:
- Read each image yourself with the Read tool — look at it carefully, zoom in via cropping with Python/PIL if a region is unclear.
- "confidence" is 0-100, your honest probability that the SMILES is exactly right (correct skeleton AND correct stereochemistry where drawn). Be calibrated: use the low end freely when you are guessing at a detail.
- "name_if_recognised" may be null if you do not recognise it.
- Include stereochemistry (@/@@, /, \) only where the drawing actually shows wedges/hashes or cis/trans geometry.
- Expand any abbreviation you can read (Me, Et, Ph, Boc, Ac, OMe, Ts, Bn, CF3, NHAc, etc.) into explicit atoms.
- Sanity-check every SMILES parses with RDKit before writing it: /root/C-MAGE/.venv-ms/bin/python -c "from rdkit import Chem; print(Chem.MolToSmiles(Chem.MolFromSmiles('...')))"
- Write all eight entries, fig01 through fig08, even if some are low confidence. Use "fig01" style keys in the "img" field.

Your final message should just say you wrote the file and give a one-line summary of your confidence spread.
